name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
title: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
answer: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of putting a question to a dataset in ordinary words and getting back a result that can be checked, rather than writing SQL or a script by hand. It sits inside quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the value is not only the answer but the path taken to reach it, which someone else must be able to follow. The scope runs from a single analyst querying a table to a team building a shared layer over a warehouse, and it includes the awkward middle ground where a question is clear to a person but ambiguous to a machine.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of putting a question to a dataset in ordinary words and getting back a result that can be checked, rather than writing SQL or a script by hand. It sits inside quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the value is not only the answer but the path taken to reach it, which someone else must be able to follow. The scope runs from a single analyst querying a table to a team building a shared layer over a warehouse, and it includes the awkward middle ground where a question is clear to a person but ambiguous to a machine.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a data store the question can reach, most often a relational warehouse or a columnar analytics database, plus a translation layer that turns the question into a query. That layer is usually a language model paired with a schema description, a set of table and column definitions, and sometimes a semantic model that fixes what terms like revenue or active customer mean. Results come back as tables or charts, and the surrounding tooling is the same as any analysis stack: version control, notebooks, a scheduler, and a place to record what was asked and what came back.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A plain language question is parsed into an intent, matched against the available tables and columns, and rendered as a query that the database executes. The hard part is not the translation but the grounding: the system needs to know which column holds the date, which join is correct, and which rows should be excluded. Good practice is to keep the generated query visible, run it against a known result where one exists, and treat the answer as a draft until a person confirms it. Reproducibility comes from storing the question, the generated query, the schema version, and the returned data together, so the same question can be re-run and compared later.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because the system reads real tables, access control follows the data rather than the interface: a person asking a question should not see rows they could not otherwise query. Generated queries can be wrong in ways that look plausible, so provenance matters, meaning the question, the query, the schema and the timestamp should travel with the result. Sensitive fields need masking or exclusion before they reach a model, and any external service used for translation becomes part of the data flow that privacy and audit reviews must cover. Ownership of a wrong answer sits with the person who published it, not with the tool that drafted it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward semantic layers that define metrics once and let both people and systems use them, which reduces the ambiguity that plain language introduces. Evaluation is maturing from spot checks toward benchmark question sets with known answers, so accuracy can be tracked rather than assumed. More questions will be answered conversationally inside existing analysis tools, which shifts the analyst's work toward defining terms, checking results, and maintaining the definitions everyone else relies on. The open question is how much of the translation can be trusted without a person in the loop, and that will be settled by practice rather than by any single release.
